title: IAsyncDisposable and async resource cleanup
description: Use IAsyncDisposable for async cleanup, understand await using, and avoid blocking on async dispose in ASP.NET Core.

data.text: Not all resources can be cleaned up synchronously. A `Stream` that writes to a network socket may need to flush a buffer and wait for the remote endpoint to acknowledge receipt. A database connection may need to commit a transaction before closing. These operations take time, and blocking a thread while they complete wastes a thread-pool thread. `IAsyncDisposable` was introduced in .NET Core 3.0 and standardized in C# 8.0 to provide a cleanup pattern that works with `await` instead of blocking.

`IAsyncDisposable` mirrors `IDisposable` but with an asynchronous `DisposeAsync` method that returns a `ValueTask`. The `await using` statement calls `DisposeAsync` and awaits the result. When `DisposeAsync` completes, all async cleanup has finished. This is especially important in ASP.NET Core, where blocking on async code can cause thread-pool starvation and deadlocks under load.

The `IAsyncDisposable` interface declares a single method: `ValueTask DisposeAsync()`. Returning `ValueTask` avoids the allocation that `Task` would create for the common case where `DisposeAsync` completes synchronously. Inside `DisposeAsync`, you await any async cleanup operations — `FlushAsync`, `CommitAsync`, `CloseAsync` — and then release unmanaged resources. If your type also holds managed resources that implement `IAsyncDisposable`, dispose them first before touching unmanaged resources.

data.title: Implementing IAsyncDisposable

data.text: await using in C# 8.0 and later

The `await using` statement works exactly like `using`, but it awaits the `DisposeAsync` call. When the `await using` block exits — whether normally or via an exception — the compiler generates a `try`/`finally` that calls `DisposeAsync` and awaits it. This means your cleanup code is exception-safe without any extra effort. In C# 11, `await using` also works with `foreach` over `IAsyncEnumerable<T>` to dispose the enumerator when iteration ends.

data.title: Using await using with an async stream

data.text: ASP.NET Core and the disposal contract

ASP.NET Core's `IHostedService` and middleware pipelines rely heavily on `IAsyncDisposable`. The generic host calls `StopAsync` on all hosted services, and `DisposeAsync` on the application container. If your hosted service or database connection class only implements `IDisposable`, the host will call `Dispose` synchronously — which may block the shutdown thread if your cleanup involves network I/O. Always implement `IAsyncDisposable` for resources that require async cleanup in ASP.NET Core applications.

data.title: Never block on async dispose
data.text: Calling `.GetAwaiter().GetResult()` or `.Wait()` inside `Dispose()` to invoke `DisposeAsync` defeats the purpose of async cleanup and can cause deadlocks in ASP.NET Core. If you must bridge sync and async cleanup, use `DisposeAsync().AsTask().GetAwaiter().GetResult()` only as a last resort, and document why it is safe in your specific context. Prefer making the entire call chain async.

data.title: Key takeaways
items: `IAsyncDisposable` provides async cleanup via `ValueTask DisposeAsync()`; use it for resources that need I/O to release.
`await using` ensures `DisposeAsync` is called and awaited, providing exception-safe async cleanup.
ASP.NET Core prefers `IAsyncDisposable` for hosted services and database connections to avoid blocking shutdown.
Never block on async dispose synchronously — it can deadlock and defeats the purpose of async cleanup.
